image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #684: We Get It

titleText.es: La forma más brutal que he visto de manejar esto fue así: —Oh, tienes una novia. ¿Vais a casaros? —Yo, eh, no lo sé... —Bien, ¿la quieres? —... —Bueno, ¿qué decías de la película?
titleText.en: The most brutal way I've ever seen someone handle this was 'Oh, you have a girlfriend. Are you going to get married?'  'I, uh, don't know--' 'Well, do you love her?' '...' 'Anyway, what were you saying about the movie?'
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive and official xkcd source both identify comic #684. The Spanish archive title text is preserved exactly, and the official English title text retains its deliberate two-space break between the first two quoted turns. OCR misread or dropped characters and accents in SÍ, VI, LA, QUÉ, ESTOY, and VIÉNDOME and omitted the first two rows of the final speech bubble; the artifact follows the visible raster, joins the printed MENCIONADO and ESTOY line wraps, and leaves their wrap hyphens as punctuation.

regions.labelEs: ¿AVATAR? SÍ, LA VI LA SEMANA PASADA CON...

excludedUnits.rationale: This unchanged film title is a proper name rather than a Spanish lexical unit.

applications.explanationEn: La replaces the feminine film title and stands immediately before the completed past verb vi.
La and pasada use feminine singular agreement with semana, and pasada follows the time noun.

regions.labelEs: ¿SABES?, SI ESTA FASE DE VUESTRA RELACIÓN DURA MÁS DE UNA SEMANA, LEGALMENTE TENGO DERECHO A APUÑALAROS A LOS DOS.

applications.explanationEn: The ordinary verb form sabes becomes a yes-or-no question through its question intonation and punctuation.
Vuestra addresses several people informally in the form used mainly in Spain and agrees with one feminine thing.

applications.exampleEs: SI ESTA FASE DE VUESTRA RELACIÓN DURA
applications.explanationEn: Si introduces a condition treated as possible, and dura uses the ordinary present form inside that condition.
Más de introduces the duration threshold, and una semana supplies the quantity being exceeded.
Legal takes -mente to form an adverb describing the claim in terms of the law.
Tengo changes for the speaker, derecho a introduces the claimed entitlement, and apuñalar remains the unchanged action inside apuñalaros.
Os attaches to the unchanged action apuñalar in one written word and identifies several informal listeners.
Attached os refers to several people addressed informally in the form used mainly in Spain.
A marks los dos as the two people who directly receive the action.
Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks which stage is meant.

regions.labelEs: BUENO, ¿HE MENCIONADO QUE ESTOY VIÉNDOME CON ALGUIEN?

applications.explanationEn: Bueno opens a new conversational move rather than describing something as good.
He matches the speaker, and mencionado supplies the completed action being brought up now.

applications.exampleEs: ¿HE MENCIONADO QUE ESTOY VIÉNDOME CON ALGUIEN?
applications.explanationEn: The complete statement order remains in place; question marks and intonation turn it into a yes-or-no question without an extra helper word.
Estoy matches the speaker, and viéndome supplies the ongoing pronominal action.
Me attaches to viendo as part of verse, and the written accent preserves the original stress.
Viéndome supplies the pronominal form for the speaker, and con alguien introduces the unnamed person being dated.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.
Vi is the completed past form of ver for yo. It can describe seeing a person or thing and also watching a film or program.

cards.questionEn: How do you say ‘last week’ when referring to the most recent completed week?
cards.noteEn: The article la and the adjective pasada both match the feminine noun semana. Spanish normally places pasada after the time noun in this expression.

example.es: Fuimos al museo la semana pasada.
example.en: We went to the museum last week.

cards.noteEn: After a feminine time word such as semana, pasada identifies the most recent completed one. With a masculine time word, use pasado: el mes pasado.
A speaker can use ¿sabes? to introduce a thought or draw the listener's attention, without literally testing what the listener knows.

example.en: You know? I think you're right.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a real or possible condition with “if”?
cards.answerEn: Use si without an accent, followed by an ordinary present-time verb form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern treats the condition as genuinely possible. Spanish normally does not put a future-tense verb directly after si in this kind of condition; the result can appear separately as a statement, prediction, or command.
Fase is a feminine noun for one stage within a longer process, project, or relationship.

example.es: El proyecto entró en una fase nueva.
example.en: The project entered a new phase.

cards.answerEn: your (informal plural in Spain; before one feminine thing)
cards.noteEn: Vuestra says that something belongs to several people addressed informally. Its feminine singular ending matches the one feminine thing owned, not the number or gender of the owners.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.noteEn: Dura is a form of durar, which describes how long something continues. It is unrelated to dura meaning “hard” when used as an adjective.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an amount is more than a particular number or quantity?
cards.answerEn: Put más de directly before the number or amount.
cards.noteEn: Use más de when the next element is a quantity being exceeded. Use más que instead when directly comparing people, things, qualities, or actions: más de diez libros, but Ana lee más que Luis.

example.en: She bought more than three books.

cards.noteEn: Before a number or other quantity, Spanish uses más de for “more than.” This de is different from más que, which commonly compares one person, thing, or action with another.

example.en: There are more than twenty people.

cards.noteEn: Legalmente is built from legal plus -mente. It describes what the law permits, requires, or recognizes.

example.en: Legally, the contract remains in force.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has the right or entitlement to perform an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of tener, then derecho a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Tener changes for the person and time. Derecho a stays together, and the following action remains in its dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir: tengo derecho a entrar, tienen derecho a votar.

example.es: Tenemos derecho a recibir una respuesta.
example.en: We have the right to receive an answer.

cards.noteEn: In tener derecho a, derecho is something a person is allowed or entitled to do. This is distinct from derecho as the direction ‘right’ or as the field of law.

example.en: Everyone has the right to rest.

cards.answerEn: to; required after tener derecho before an action
cards.noteEn: The expression tener derecho uses a before the allowed action. The following action verb stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: You have the right to ask.

cards.answerEn: to stab you all; to stab both of you (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Apuñalar is the unchanged action verb ‘to stab.’ Attached os identifies several people addressed informally, and the two parts are written as one word.

example.es: En la obra, el villano amenaza con apuñalaros.
example.en: In the play, the villain threatens to stab you all.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a person-denoting object
cards.noteEn: The personal a also appears before words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) when they directly receive an action, even though they do not identify one specific individual.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.answerEn: It can mean “well…,” giving the speaker time or softening the reply.
cards.noteEn: Here bueno organizes the conversation rather than describing a person or thing. A pause after it can signal hesitation, reluctance, or a gentle correction.
cards.questionEn: What can bueno mean at the start of an answer when it is not describing something as good?

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Mencionado is the completed-action form of mencionar. After he, it says that the speaker has mentioned something.
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Viéndome is the ongoing-action form of verse with me attached for the speaker. In a romantic context, verse con alguien can mean to be seeing or dating someone. The written accent keeps the original stress after me is added.

example.es: Estoy viéndome con alguien desde mayo.
example.en: I have been seeing someone since May.

cards.questionEn: How do you attach the matching marker of a pronominal verb to an ongoing-action form?
cards.answerEn: Join me, te, se, nos, os, or se to the end of the -ando or -iendo form, adding a written accent when needed to preserve the original stress.
cards.noteEn: A pronominal verb is learned with se, such as verse or prepararse. Its short marker changes with the person. When the marker follows an ongoing-action form as one word, spelling may need an accent: viendo + me becomes viéndome, and preparando + se becomes preparándose.

example.en: I am getting ready to leave.

cards.questionEn: How can you say that someone is seeing or dating another person?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of verse, then con and the other person.
cards.noteEn: The short marker changes with the subject: me veo, te ves, se ve, nos vemos, os veis, se ven. The romantic meaning comes from context; the same structure can simply mean meeting or seeing someone.

example.es: Ana se está viendo con alguien.

cards.answerEn: with; required after verse before the other person
cards.noteEn: Verse con introduces the person someone meets, sees, or dates. Con stays the same for every person and time.

example.es: Marta se ve con Luis los viernes.
